title: What Is a Deductible? How It Works in Your Health Insurance
summary: What is a deductible? Learn how a health insurance deductible works, what counts toward it, family vs. individual deductibles, and 2026 HDHP minimums.
body_markdown:
If you've ever opened a medical bill and wondered why you owed the full amount even though you have health insurance, the answer is almost always your deductible. This guide explains what a deductible is, how it fits into your health plan, what counts toward it, and how to plan for it when you pick a plan during open enrollment.


## What is a deductible?


A health insurance deductible is the amount you pay out of your own pocket for covered health care services each plan year before your health plan starts sharing costs with you. For example, if your plan has a $2,000 annual deductible, you pay the first $2,000 of covered medical expenses yourself. After that, your insurance company starts paying its share, and you pay a copay or coinsurance instead.


Deductibles show up in employer-sponsored plans, ACA marketplace plans, and many Medicare plans. Other types of insurance use deductibles too. Auto, homeowners, and renters insurance deductibles usually apply per claim, while a health insurance deductible applies to your total covered costs across the plan year and resets when a new plan year begins.


Your deductible is separate from your monthly premium, which you pay whether or not you use any medical services. It's also different from your out-of-pocket maximum, which caps what you'll spend on covered care in a plan year.


## Deductible basics: How they fit into your health plan


A few health insurance terms work together in every plan. Here's how they connect.


- **Covered services:** the medical services, treatments, and prescription drugs your plan agrees to help pay for.
- **Deductible:** the fixed amount you pay for covered services in a plan year before cost sharing begins.
- **Copay:** a flat fee you pay per service, like $25 for a doctor visit.
- **Coinsurance:** the percentage of the allowed cost you pay after meeting your deductible, such as 20%.
- **Out-of-pocket maximum:** the ceiling on your total cost sharing for covered, in-network care in a plan year.


Here's how it flows in a typical plan year starting January 1. You pay 100% of the allowed cost for covered care until you meet your deductible amount. After that, you pay coinsurance or copays while your insurance company pays its share. Once your deductible, copays, and coinsurance add up to the out-of-pocket maximum, your plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the year.


Deductibles usually apply to in-network care. Out-of-network care often has a separate, higher deductible, and some plans don't count out-of-network payments toward your main deductible at all.


Deductibles reset every plan year. Most employer and marketplace plans reset on January 1, but some employers run benefit years on different dates, like July 1 through June 30. Once you reach your deductible, insurance starts covering costs, but that progress disappears when the new plan year begins.


## Deductible vs. premium vs. out-of-pocket maximum


These three costs make up the financial backbone of any health insurance plan, and they're the numbers to compare during open enrollment.


- **Premium:** what you pay every month to keep your insurance coverage active, whether you visit a doctor or not. Premiums never count toward your deductible.
- **Deductible:** what you pay for covered medical services before your insurance plan starts paying its share.
- **Out-of-pocket maximum:** the most you'll pay in a plan year for covered in-network services, including your deductible, coinsurance, and copays. Once you hit it, your plan covers 100%.


Here's an example plan: a $450 monthly premium ($5,400 a year), a $2,500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $7,500 out-of-pocket limit. You pay the premium every month. If you need $2,500 in covered care, you pay that in full. After that, you pay 20% of additional covered costs. Once your deductible, coinsurance, and copays reach $7,500, you owe nothing more for covered in-network services that year. For a closer look at how the two limits interact, see our guide to[deductible vs. out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) .


## How deductibles work in practice


The mechanics are easier to follow with real numbers. Say your plan has a $2,000 deductible with 20% coinsurance after that.


You need an MRI. The facility bills $1,500, but your plan's negotiated allowed amount with that in-network provider is $1,000. Because you haven't met your deductible, you pay the $1,000 allowed amount, not the $1,500 sticker price, and that $1,000 counts toward your deductible.


Later you have $1,000 of covered specialist care, which brings you to your $2,000 deductible. Then a $600 lab test comes along. Now cost sharing applies: you pay 20% ($120) and your insurance company pays the remaining $480. You keep paying coinsurance on covered services until you reach your out-of-pocket maximum, at which point the plan covers everything.


Two exceptions are worth knowing:


- **Preventive care.** Under the Affordable Care Act, most plans must cover a set of[preventive services](https://www.healthcare.gov/preventive-care-adults/) , such as annual wellness visits, immunizations, and certain screenings, at no cost when you use an in-network provider, even if you haven't paid anything toward your deductible.
- **Prescription drugs.** Some health plans have a separate deductible for prescription drugs. A plan might have a $2,000 medical deductible and a $500 drug deductible, so you pay the first $500 of covered prescription costs before drug copays or coinsurance apply.


## What costs count toward my deductible?


Most covered medical services count toward your deductible, including visits to your primary care doctor, specialist appointments, lab tests, imaging, urgent care visits, emergency room trips, surgeries, and inpatient hospital stays. If it's a covered service under your insurance plan and the claim goes through your insurer, it generally counts.


Only the allowed amount counts. If an out-of-network provider charges more than your plan's allowed amount and bills you for the difference (balance billing), that extra amount typically doesn't count toward your deductible.


Your insurer tracks these amounts for you. You can usually see your deductible status in your insurance provider's online portal or app. Costs count only once claims are processed, so there may be a short lag between your office visit and when it appears on your account.


## What does not count toward my deductible?


Several common health care expenses never reduce your deductible, no matter how much you spend on them:


- **Monthly premiums.** They keep your coverage active but are separate from deductibles, copays, and coinsurance.
- **Services your plan doesn't cover.** Elective cosmetic procedures, treatments your plan deems not medically necessary, and anything your plan excludes won't move you closer to meeting your deductible.
- **Charges above the allowed amount.** If an out-of-network provider bills $2,000 but your plan's allowed amount is $1,200, the $800 difference is usually your responsibility and won't apply toward your deductible.
- **Fees outside your plan,** such as missed-appointment or late-cancellation charges.


Copays depend on your plan. Many plans charge a copay for services like a doctor's office visit from day one, without counting it toward the deductible; others apply it. Copays almost always count toward your out-of-pocket maximum. Check your Summary of Benefits and Coverage to see how your plan handles them.


## Individual vs. family deductible explained


If your plan covers more than just yourself, how individual and family deductibles interact matters for your[family's](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-dependents-spouse-family-friends) health care costs.


A family deductible is the total amount all family members on the plan must pay combined before the plan starts sharing costs for everyone. Family plans handle it in one of two ways:


- **Embedded deductible:** each person has an individual deductible inside the family deductible. Take a four-person family with a $2,500 individual deductible and a $10,000 family deductible. If one child has $2,500 in covered medical costs, cost sharing starts for that child right away, even though the family deductible hasn't been met.
- **Non-embedded (aggregate) deductible:** there's no individual deductible. The family must meet the full family deductible together before cost sharing starts for anyone. With a $6,000 aggregate deductible, no one gets cost sharing until the family's combined covered costs reach $6,000, no matter who incurred them.


Either way, what each person pays toward their own deductible also counts toward the family deductible. The difference matters most when one family member has much higher medical needs than the others.


## High deductible health plans (HDHPs) and HSAs


A high deductible health plan (HDHP) is a type of health insurance plan that meets[IRS requirements](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) for pairing with a health savings account (HSA). The IRS updates the minimum deductible and out-of-pocket limits each year.


For 2026, an HDHP must have a deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage, and its out-of-pocket maximum can't exceed $8,500 (self-only) or $17,000 (family). For 2027, those figures rise to a $1,750 / $3,500 minimum deductible and an $8,700 / $17,400 out-of-pocket maximum.


HDHPs usually have lower monthly premiums than traditional plans, but you pay more out of pocket before coverage starts. They often suit people with low expected medical needs who could cover a higher deductible if something came up. Like other ACA-compliant plans, HDHPs cover preventive care before the deductible.


An[HSA](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) lets you contribute pre-tax dollars and withdraw them tax-free for qualified medical expenses, including deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. Unused HSA funds roll over from year to year, and the account stays with you if you change jobs. To weigh an HDHP against a traditional plan, see[PPO vs. HDHP](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ppo-vs-hdhp) .


## Low deductible health plans and when they make sense


A low deductible health plan has a deductible well below the IRS minimum for an HDHP, so your insurance starts paying its share earlier in the year. The trade-off is a higher monthly premium.


Low deductible plans tend to work for people who need frequent medical care, such as someone managing a chronic condition like diabetes who sees a doctor regularly, takes monthly medications, and visits specialists several times a year. If you're planning a surgery or expecting a baby, paying more in premiums each month may cost less overall than meeting a large deductible on top of coinsurance.


A low deductible plan doesn't let you contribute to an HSA, because the deductible falls below the IRS minimum. You may still be able to use a health care FSA or a health reimbursement arrangement (HRA) if your employer offers one.


## Choosing a deductible: How to decide what's right for you


Picking a deductible isn't about finding the "best" plan. It's about the best plan for your situation this year.


1. **Review last year's health care use.** Count doctor visits, specialist appointments, prescriptions, urgent care trips, and procedures. If you rarely see a doctor, a higher deductible with lower premiums may work. If you see a doctor regularly or take ongoing medications, a lower deductible often makes more sense.
2. **Check your financial cushion.** Could you cover the full deductible, or even the out-of-pocket maximum, if a large medical bill arrived unexpectedly? If not, a lower deductible gives you more predictable costs.
3. **Compare total annual cost.** Add premiums to expected out-of-pocket costs. Compare a plan with a $250 monthly premium and a $3,000 deductible against one with a $400 monthly premium and a $1,000 deductible. If you expect $4,000 in covered care, the totals (including coinsurance) may be closer than the premium difference suggests. Run the numbers for low, moderate, and high usage during[open enrollment](https://www.withflex.com/blog/your-2026-open-enrollment-cheat-sheet-7-terms-you-actually-need-to-know) .
4. **Look at the family structure.** If one family member has much higher needs, an embedded deductible lets that person reach cost sharing sooner.
5. **Count your tax-advantaged accounts.** If you have access to an HSA, HRA, or FSA, factor those[pre-tax contributions](https://www.withflex.com/blog/are-hsa-contributions-tax-deductible) into your planning.


## How HSAs, FSAs, and HRAs help you handle deductibles


These three account types let you pay deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and other qualified medical expenses with pre-tax money.


- **Health savings account (HSA):** you contribute pre-tax income, it can grow tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. HSA funds[don't expire](https://www.withflex.com/blog/use-or-lose-hsa-expire) and stay with you if you leave your employer. You need a qualifying HDHP to contribute.
- **Flexible spending account (FSA):** funded with pre-tax payroll deductions through your employer. FSAs generally follow[use-it-or-lose-it rules](https://www.withflex.com/blog/use-or-lose-fsa-expire) , though some plans offer a grace period or a limited carryover.
- **Health reimbursement arrangement (HRA):** funded by your employer, which decides what it reimburses. Depending on the plan, that can include deductible payments.


One simple approach: during open enrollment, estimate your expected medical costs for the year, then set your HSA or FSA contribution with your deductible in mind. That way, when a medical bill arrives early in the plan year, you can pay it from pre-tax dollars instead of after-tax cash. To see what else those funds can cover, browse our[FSA eligible items list](https://www.withflex.com/blog/fsa-eligible-items-list) .


## Practical tips for tracking and managing your deductible


- **Check your progress.** Log in to your health plan's website or app to see how much of your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum you've met so far this plan year.
- **Keep records.** Save explanations of benefits (EOBs) and receipts for major health care expenses so you can confirm costs were applied correctly and catch billing errors.
- **Time necessary care.** If you've met your deductible late in the year, scheduling needed care before the plan year resets means you'll pay only coinsurance or copays instead of the full allowed amount.
- **Ask when unsure.** If your Summary of Benefits and Coverage doesn't make it clear how copays or out-of-network care count, call the customer service number on your insurance card.
- **Coordinate your accounts.** If you use an HSA, FSA, or HRA, match your balance to upcoming appointments so you know what you can pay with pre-tax funds.


Knowing your deductible turns a surprise medical bill into a cost you planned for. Take a few minutes to look up your plan's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, check what you've met so far, and decide how much to set aside in a tax-advantaged account for the year ahead.
